interactions.summary: Jiang answers the student's suicide objection by saying Catholic suicide doctrine does not straightforwardly govern this Hebrew or Israelite story, then closes the exchange and returns to the text.
A student reads Beatrice's lines condemning the stupidity of doing worse by keeping faith, including the comparison between Jephthah and Agamemnon.

Jiang glosses the paradoxical line, then retells the Agamemnon and Iphigenia story as a second example of vow-keeping stupidity, ending with a student correctly recalling that Clytemnestra avenged the daughter's death.

claims.claim: Jiang says the student's suicide objection cannot simply be resolved by later Catholic doctrine because the Jephthah story belongs to a Hebrew or Israelite cultural world rather than the Catholic one.
Jiang reads Beatrice's line about doing worse by keeping faith as naming a real paradox: vow-keeping can become morally more stupid than vow-breaking when literal obedience destroys innocent life.
Jiang says Beatrice treats Jephthah and Agamemnon as parallel cases of stupidity because both men let an oath or obligation override basic moral judgment.

In Jiang's retelling, the Greek coalition binds itself by oath to defend Helen's marriage, and that preexisting vow becomes the reason Agamemnon feels compelled to appease Artemis and continue the war expedition.
Jiang judges Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia as stupid because he should have been able to foresee that murdering a beloved daughter would provoke retaliatory destruction inside his own house.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang stops on Dante's strange moral formula that one can do worse by keeping faith than by breaking it.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the seminar a compact principle for judging vows by moral intelligence rather than by empty literalism.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice's two canonical fools become Jephthah and Agamemnon, a biblical judge and a Greek king united by oath-driven stupidity.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there are two really stupid people in this world
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Jiang uses the pairing to widen the packet from one biblical anomaly into a broader civilizational warning about vows and judgment.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reduces Beatrice's teaching to a blunt command: keep your vows to the gods if you must, but use your brains.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's cleanest moral compression and keeps Jiang's anti-literalist heat intact.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's gloss on Beatrice's paradox that literal fidelity to a vow can become morally inferior to breaking it when obedience causes greater evil.
Jiang's blunt shorthand for Beatrice's teaching that vows must be judged with intelligence and foresight rather than kept mechanically.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet closes the Jephthah suicide objection and generalizes the vow problem through Agamemnon: Jiang moves from one biblical case to a cross-tradition pattern in which formal oath-keeping becomes stupid when it overrides moral judgment and predictable consequences.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's answer to the suicide objection is brief and somewhat hand-waving; the secure point is that he suspends straightforward Catholic categorization rather than fully resolving the doctrinal issue.
